rewriteLast.title: Chapter 8 · The Kind Doctor
rewriteLast.artPrompt: a small girl with sunny braids carrying a basket of clover walking along a dusty Vermont lane beside a gentleman doctor on a brown horse, white fences and wildflowers, warm morning light, storybook illustration

blocks.text: One bright morning Pollyanna set out for town with a basket of clover for Mrs. Snow. Behind her came the roll of carriage wheels, and a gentleman drew his horse down to a walk beside her. He had grey eyes and a kind, sun-brown face. It was Dr. Chilton, the best doctor in the county, and he lifted his hat as politely as if she were a lady. "Good morning!" he said. "And where are you bound, with all that clover?"

Pollyanna told him everything — about Mrs. Snow, about the clover, and about Beldingsville, the friendliest town in the world. Then he asked who she might be. "I am Pollyanna Whittier," she said proudly, "and I live with my Aunt Polly." The doctor's smile went quiet, like a lamp behind a cloud. He looked away at the far green hills for a moment. Then he said only that it was a fine morning for walking, and not one word more about aunts.
Dr. Chilton walking his horse slowly beside Pollyanna and her basket of clover.

That evening Pollyanna asked Nancy about the grey-eyed doctor. Nancy set down her dishcloth and sighed. "That is Dr. Chilton, dear. The best doctor for fifty miles — and the loneliest man in Beldingsville. He and your Aunt Polly were dear friends once, long before you were born. Then came a bitter quarrel, and neither of them would say sorry. The years just walked away, and the two of them let them go."
New word: quarrel — an angry argument that lasts too long. A quarrel that nobody mends grows old with the people who keep it.

Pollyanna lay in the attic and thought about it into the dark. Two dear friends, and years of silence — how lonely, how wasteful! "Somebody must help them play again," she told the ceiling. "Quarrels are such lonely things to live in." She made a small, patient plan, as tiny as a seed and just as quiet. She did not know how very soon that little seed would come to matter.

chapters.title: Chapter 9 · A Home for Jimmy
chapters.artPrompt: a ragged boy now scrubbed and neat standing proudly on the doorstep of a big grey stone house beside a smiling elderly gentleman, a small girl with braids clapping her hands on the garden path, bright morning light, storybook illustration

blocks.text: News ran through Beldingsville like wind through ripe wheat: Jimmy Bean had gone to live at Mr. Pendleton's. The barn-loft boy had a real bed now, and books on a shelf, and somebody to say good night to. Every morning a boy's whistle floated out of the big house by the common, and nobody minded it one bit. Mr. Pendleton was cross no longer — he was far too busy being a father. Beldingsville took the news two ways: amazement first, and then, very quickly, pride. If a cross old gentleman could open his heart, whose door was safe from a glad little girl?

Jimmy came bouncing to the white house to tell Pollyanna all about it. "You begged the Ladies' Aid for me when nobody else would," he said. "And now look! Mr. Pendleton says a home isn't a roof — it's somebody being glad you're there. Well, I'm the somebody, and he's mine, and I'm his!" Pollyanna clapped her hands until her basket swung. Her little game had made a whole family.
Jimmy on the doorstep of his new home, with Mr. Pendleton smiling behind him.
A home is more than four walls and a bed. It is somebody being glad you came. Whose somebody could you be this week?

On Sunday, Jimmy sat in the great pew beside Mr. Pendleton, scrubbed and shining and proud as a deacon. Aunt Polly looked across the church at the two of them. Her face stayed as stiff as ever, but her eyes were soft as spring rain. "The game spreads," Pollyanna whispered to herself happily. "It spreads and spreads, and nobody can stop it now."

After church Jimmy waited at the gate to walk home with her. "Pollyanna," he said very seriously, "when I'm rich, I'm going to find some other fellow with no home. And I'm going to say what you said. About finding the glad part first." Pollyanna beamed at him. "That IS the game!" she cried. "And you learned it without even a barrel of crutches!"

chapters.title: Chapter 10 · The Long Quarrel
chapters.artPrompt: a tall elderly woman in black standing very straight at a dark parlour window at night, looking down an empty moonlit road toward distant cottage lights, a small girl peeking round the door, quiet blue shadows, storybook illustration

blocks.text: Pollyanna could not stop thinking about Aunt Polly and Dr. Chilton. One evening she asked Nancy why people let quarrels grow so old. Nancy dried a plate slowly, choosing her words. "Pride, dear," she said at last. "Pride is when you would rather be right than be glad. It stands at the door with folded arms and calls itself strength. And it keeps out the very people you want most."

So Pollyanna began her little gardening. At supper she said, casually as anything, that Dr. Chilton had the gentlest hands in the county, and walked his horse so carefully that no child was ever frightened. Aunt Polly went still as a statue. "We do not discuss Dr. Chilton at this table," she said. But she did not say stop. And in that house, Nancy agreed, that was very nearly a conversation.
Aunt Polly at the parlour window, watching the dark road where the doctor's gig sometimes passed.
Have you ever waited too long to say sorry? The longer you wait, the heavier the little word feels. Small sorries are best said soon.

That night, passing the parlour door, Pollyanna saw Aunt Polly standing at the window, looking down the dark road. She stood a long, long time, very straight and very still. Nobody in the house knew what she was thinking. But she did not light the lamp, and she did not go to bed, and the road stayed empty all night long. In the morning her eyes were tired, and her greetings at breakfast were short. Proud people pay for their pride in private, Pollyanna decided. The bill comes when nobody is watching.

Pollyanna went upstairs and watered her seed with hope. Someday, somehow, those two proud people would be friends again — she had promised the ceiling, and the ceiling never forgot. Then she snuggled down under the quilts and fell asleep planning kindnesses. That is the very best way of all to fall asleep. Somewhere down the hill a light burned late in a doctor's window. Two lamps, two houses, one long quarrel — and a very small girl with a very patient plan, dreaming between them.

chapters.title: Chapter 11 · The Accident
chapters.artPrompt: a bright village square on a Saturday morning with a stopped early motor car at the corner and townspeople running from doorways, a small straw hat and scattered clover lying in the road, dramatic warm light, storybook illustration

blocks.text: It was a bright Saturday morning, and the square was full of Saturday sounds — wagons, voices, church bells far away. Pollyanna crossed the road by the common, thinking about Mrs. Snow's jelly. Then a motor car came whizzing round the corner, fast, far too fast. There was a shout, a screech, a terrible jolt — and the bright morning went suddenly dark. The driver leaped out, white-faced, shouting for help. The basket rolled into the gutter, and the clover scattered across the bright road like small green tears.

People came running from every door. Gentle hands lifted her and carried her home to the big white house, and the town doctor came at once, galloping. He worked over her for hours, while Aunt Polly sat outside the door, white as marble and perfectly still. Pollyanna had been hurt before, and had always mended. Everybody could see that this time was different. Beldingsville went quiet all at once, and quiet is a loud sound in a small town.
The crowd gathered round the stopped motor car in the bright Saturday square.
New word: motor car — a horseless carriage. In Pollyanna's day they were brand new, and drivers had not yet learned to be careful.

Word travelled down the hill and along every street of Beldingsville, and it seemed that every door in town opened at once. People came out onto their porches and stood quietly, looking toward the white house on the hill. Nobody said the word hope out loud. Everybody was thinking it.

Evening came, and a lamp burned low in the sick room. The girl who was glad about everything lay very still among the pillows, pale as the pillow itself. She did not know the voices around her. Downstairs the clock ticked on and on. The big white house was silent as stone, from attic to porch. Upstairs a candle burned low beside the bed. A tall dark figure sat beside it without moving, holding one small hand tight.

chapters.title: Chapter 12 · The Best Doctor
chapters.artPrompt: a tired grey-eyed doctor standing beside his lathered horse at the lamplit door of a big white house at night, a tall woman in black holding the door open, rain clouds parting, storybook illustration

blocks.text: The town doctor came down at last, and his face said the verdict before his mouth did. "This is beyond me," he said quietly. "If anyone can help her, it is Chilton. He is the best there is." Aunt Polly stood very straight and very pale. Then she said the name she had not spoken aloud in years. "Send for Dr. Chilton." Pride went down like a flag. It had flown over that house for years, stiff and high. Now it came down in one morning, for a little girl.

Dr. Chilton came within the hour, bag in hand, his horse lathered from the long climb. He worked through the night, soft-footed and tireless. When he passed Aunt Polly in the corridor they spoke only of Pollyanna. Quick, low words about the hurt and the chances. But something in their eyes was gentler than it had been for years. The old quarrel's door stood open, just a crack. Twice in the night Aunt Polly carried coffee out to him with her own hands. Nancy saw it from the stairs. She said nothing at all, but her heart drummed like rain on a roof.
Dr. Chilton's tired horse waiting at the lamplit door, long past midnight.
Pride is a heavy stone to carry. Love gives people the strength to set it down — sometimes just in time.

At dawn he told Aunt Polly the truth, gently and low. The legs had been badly crushed. Only time could tell whether Pollyanna would ever walk again. "Then time shall have all the help we can give it," said Aunt Polly. Her voice did not shake until the door had closed. Then she leaned her forehead against the panel and wept like anyone.

The grey-eyed doctor was terribly tired and terribly gentle. "She has a heart like a church bell," he told Nancy. "It is rung hard, and it rings true." Nancy understood exactly, and cried a little, and went to put the kettle on. Above them all, the small patient slept on, and did not yet know.

chapters.title: Chapter 13 · When the Game Stopped
chapters.artPrompt: a small girl turned toward the wall in a dim bedroom, her bright braids loose on the pillow, a tall elderly woman keeping watch in a chair by the window, grey winter light through half-closed blinds, storybook illustration

blocks.text: The days went by, and everyone's smiles grew careful — smiles put on like Sunday clothes. Pollyanna was nobody's fool. She heard the whispers at her door, and saw the grave faces bending over her. So one morning she asked straight out: "Aunt Polly, tell me truly. Will I ever walk again?" The room went terribly silent. Then Aunt Polly's tears fell on the small hand she was holding, and that said everything.

For the first time since her father taught her, Pollyanna could not find one glad thing. Not one. She turned her face to the wall. She did not ask about the garden, or the kitten, or the weather. She did not sing. The glad game had stopped — and the whole house felt the cold of it, like a window left open in winter. Her glads had always been like pennies in a pocket. She had never once found the pocket empty. Now she searched, and searched, and her fingers came up still.
Pollyanna turned to the wall, with Aunt Polly keeping watch beside the bed.
Even the gladdest people have days with no gladness in them. That does not mean the game is broken. It means the player is heart-tired, and needs her friends.

Outside, the town went on with its business and could not settle to it. The grocer weighed sugar wrong twice. Mr. Pendleton walked over the hill with Jimmy and stood looking at the white house without saying a word. Even the kitten sat on the windowsill, waiting for a small bright voice that did not come.

Nancy cried into her apron by the stove. Dr. Chilton shook his head at the foot of the stairs. And Aunt Polly had never begged anyone for anything in all her proud life. Now she sat by the bed and would not leave it. "Come back to us," she whispered into the dark. "Oh, my dear, come back and be glad." The clock ticked. The fire settled. And far up under the roof, the attic room with the beautiful view stood empty and dark. It waited for a laugh that did not come.

chapters.title: Chapter 14 · The Whole Town Comes
chapters.artPrompt: a bedroom doorway crowded with kindly villagers bringing baskets, bouquets and covered dishes, an old gentleman with roses and a boy holding his cap, a small girl propped on pillows watching, golden afternoon light, storybook illustration

blocks.text: Then Beldingsville remembered everything the little girl had given it, and came to give it back. Visitors began to arrive — shyly at first, then in a stream that never quite dried up. Mr. Pendleton came with roses and Jimmy, who held his cap in both hands and could not say anything at all. The Ladies' Aid arrived with fruit and flowers and cocoa and forty kinds of kindness. They came up the hill in twos and threes all day long. Aunt Polly set a table by the door just for leaving things on.

And one by one, they told her what her game had done. The grocer said his Sundays were lonely no more. Old Mrs. Tarbell admitted — actually admitted — that she had laughed twice before breakfast. Mrs. Snow sent jelly with a note: 'Made by a lady who is playing the game again. You taught me, dear. Now I shall play it back to you.' Every gift carried a story with it, and every story was the game, wearing its Sunday clothes.
The doorway full of neighbors, and the bed full of flowers and love.
When someone is very sad, you cannot always fix the sadness. You can always show up — and showing up is half the cure.

Dr. Chilton let them come a few at a time, because he understood the medicine in them. Kind voices are medicine. So are roses, and jelly, and a boy who reads aloud in a serious voice with his finger under every word. The room filled up with love, day after day, like a jar filling with honey.

But at night, when the visitors were gone, the girl in the bed still watched it all from somewhere far inside herself. Aunt Polly saw it, and her heart ached worse than her tired feet. Not yet, the grey eyes said to her, gently. Not yet. So she held the small hand tighter, and learned what the whole town had learned. Love is patient. Gladness is a crop. Even the hardest field comes green again in time.

chapters.title: Chapter 15 · The Game Comes Back
chapters.artPrompt: a small girl lying in a dark bedroom counting glad things on her fingers, her eyes shining at the ceiling, moonlight through the curtain gap, a ray of silver light across the quilt, storybook illustration

blocks.text: One quiet afternoon, when the room was almost empty, Jimmy leaned close to the bed. "Pollyanna," he said, "you told me to play the glad game once, when I had nobody in the world. It's your turn now, isn't it?" She looked at him a long, long time. He did not wait for an answer. Boys his age cannot bear too long a silence beside a bed. But the seed had been planted, and seeds do not mind the dark. That, after all, is what the dark is for.

That night, alone with the dark, she began to count. Very slowly. Glad my legs ran and skipped for eleven whole years. Glad Aunt Polly loves me — and now I KNOW she loves me. Glad I taught so many people to play. Glad so many people came to play it back to me. Glad I can still think glad thoughts for others, even lying quite still. The count went slowly, like beads through tired fingers. But bead by bead the little chain of glads grew longer, and somewhere along it the dark began to shine.
Pollyanna counting her glads on her fingers in the moonlight, eyes shining.
The glad game is hardest exactly when you need it most. That is how you know it is the real game, and not just pretending.

In the morning, the sunshine was back in her voice. "Nancy!" she called, so suddenly that the tray nearly flew. "Glad there is such a lot of morning left — and glad it is EGG morning!" The whole house heard her, and the whole house glowed. The game had come home at last — carried by a whole town, and found again in one small brave heart. At breakfast Aunt Polly watched her over the top of her cup and said nothing at all. But that afternoon she ordered new curtains for the sick room — yellow ones, the color of morning.

chapters.title: Chapter 16 · Little Hopes
chapters.artPrompt: a grey-eyed doctor kneeling gently by a small girl's bed holding her foot while she looks down amazed at her own wiggling toe, a tall woman smiling behind him, soft morning light through lace curtains, storybook illustration

blocks.text: The weeks became months, and the months were made of patience. Dr. Chilton came every day with gentle exercises, steady as sunrise. Aunt Polly read aloud by the hour, in her very best voice. Some days the work hurt, and some days it was dull. Pollyanna played the game through all of it, glad even of the ache. An ache means the leg is awake, she said. Dr. Chilton called her the best patient in the county. Aunt Polly called her brave. Jimmy called her a champion. Pollyanna herself called it school, and said she meant to be top of the class.

Then, one gray Tuesday, it happened. Pollyanna's big toe moved — on purpose, all by itself. Such a tiny thing, and such a shout! Nancy dropped the spoon into the soup. Mr. Pendleton, hearing the news, sent up a basket of apples with a card that said: FOR THE TOE. Dr. Chilton smiled until his eyes crinkled. "Tiny," he said, "but true. Tiny and true."
The great morning of the little toe that moved all by itself.
New word: patience — hoping bravely while slow things happen. Legs learn to walk the way seeds learn to grow: slowly, and then all at once.

Little by little, the feeling came back. A toe. A foot. A knee that bent. Each small sign was named aloud, counted, and celebrated like a birthday. "Three signs!" Pollyanna announced one evening, holding up three fingers and beaming. The glad game played on in the sick room — and it had more players every single week. Even the kitten was allowed in now, on strictest good behavior. It slept in the exact middle of the quilt, like a small gray anchor.

In the kitchen, Nancy baked bread with extra care. In the village, people breathed more easily. Somewhere in the big white house, the hardest winter in years was turning, slowly and surely, into spring. And everyone in Beldingsville knew exactly whose courage was turning it.

chapters.title: Chapter 17 · A Wedding in the Garden
chapters.artPrompt: a garden wedding under golden maple trees, a tall bride in grey silk and a grey-eyed doctor holding hands, a small girl in a white dress with rose petals in her hair watching from a big chair, neighbors throwing petals, warm autumn light, storybook illustration

blocks.text: All that autumn, over a small patient bed, two proud people had grown humble together. They spoke of Pollyanna only, but kindness had swept the old quarrel out of every corner. The whole house felt lighter for it. Then one evening, watching Aunt Polly's face in the firelight, Dr. Chilton asked her to marry him. She said yes before he had even finished asking. After years and years of pride, it had taken one small girl and one long autumn. Between them, they had taught two proud people the shortest, hardest word of all.

They were married in the garden, between the last roses and the first snow, just as the maples turned gold. The whole town came, from the oldest grandmother to the youngest baby. There were petals to throw and bells to ring and a wedding cake taller than the kitten. Nobody remembered ever seeing Beldingsville so glad. Nancy wore her good dress and cried before anything even started. Old Tom tied the garlands himself, with shaking hands and enormous pride.
The garden wedding, with the whole town playing its happiest game.
It is never too late to begin again. Some doors only need one brave knock — even after long, long years.

Pollyanna watched from a big chair under the trees, wearing white and a crown of rose petals, prouder than anybody there. "Why," said Nancy, wiping her eyes on her apron, "Miss Polly looks ten years younger and a hundred years kinder." The stiffest lady in Beldingsville had learned the gladdest lesson of all. And the little girl in the chair had known it first.

At the wedding supper, Pollyanna lifted her glass of milk. "To the gladdest autumn ever!" she said. Dr. Chilton raised his cup solemnly to her, and Aunt Polly laughed — actually laughed, out loud, right at the table. Nancy nearly dropped the potatoes, and loved every minute of it. Late that night, Pollyanna lay awake a while, listening to the house. It did not sound stiff anymore. It sounded like a place where a glad game could grow up.

chapters.title: Chapter 18 · Learning to Walk
chapters.artPrompt: a small girl in a nightgown taking shaky first steps between a grey-eyed doctor's strong hands, a maid cheering in the doorway with her apron flying, a tall woman with both hands pressed to her heart, bright winter morning light, storybook illustration

blocks.text: Winter was a schoolroom, and courage was the lesson. Day after day, Dr. Chilton stood Pollyanna on her feet between his two strong hands. Her knees shook like new lambs. Some days she laughed, and some days she cried, and some days she did both at once. But every single day, she tried. The canes stood in the corner like patient friends. The exercises had names, like 'toe circles' and 'knee bends.' Pollyanna gave the hard ones her very best scowl, and did them anyway.

Then, one bright morning, she took a step. Then another. Then another — and the whole house came running, and everybody was talking and laughing and crying at the same time. Nancy threw her apron into the air. Aunt Polly stood in the doorway with both hands pressed against her heart, too full for one single word. Jimmy heard the news at Mr. Pendleton's and ran the whole way over the common. He arrived too late to see it, and insisted on seeing it twice the next day.
The first brave steps across the sunlit floor, with the whole household cheering.
Big victories are made of tiny tries, one after another, on the very days you feel like stopping.

Every day she went a little farther. Chair to window. Window to door. At last, with two canes, down the long garden path and back again, while the household counted her steps like birthdays. Dr. Chilton walked beside her the whole way, pretending very hard that he was not holding his breath. Winter turned. The steps grew surer. By the first thaw the canes were needed only on frosty mornings, and Pollyanna declared them excellent company anyway.

At the gate she leaned on her canes, breathless and shining. "Will I really be as quick as before?" she asked. "Better," said the doctor. "Because you will never take one single step for granted again." Pollyanna laughed her brightest laugh. "Glad steps!" she cried. "Glad, glad steps!" And she said it twice more, because once did not seem half enough.

chapters.title: Chapter 19 · The Gladdest Game of All
chapters.artPrompt: a small girl walking down a sunny garden path on her own two feet while neighbors wave from doorways and a boy and old gentleman cross the green toward her, a tall couple watching hand in hand from the porch, roses along the lane, golden summer light, storybook illustration

blocks.text: Summer came again to Beldingsville, and the roses opened all along the lane. And on a golden morning, Pollyanna Whittier walked out of the big white house — slowly, proudly, on her own two feet. She went all the way to the gate and back. People came out of their doors just to wave at her. The town had never been so glad about so small a walk. Children ran along beside her. Old ladies came out in their shawls. Somebody's baby was held up to see, and waved its fat hand, and everybody declared it had understood everything.

Jimmy and Mr. Pendleton crossed the common to walk beside her. Jimmy carried her basket, which he called the highest honor of his life. Mrs. Snow waved from her window with a ribbon in her hair. The kitten sat on the fence post like a very small lion. And Aunt Polly and Dr. Chilton watched from the porch, hand in hand.
Pollyanna walking in the sunshine, with the whole town glad around her.
The glad game never runs out. It is the one game where everybody who plays it wins.

The little girl with the carpetbag had taught a whole town to look twice for the good. In attics, in rainy picnics, in cross old gentlemen, even in sorrow. And the game went on, from door to door and heart to heart, in Beldingsville and far, far beyond it. Grocers still weighed sugar wrong on glad days. Mrs. Tarbell still laughed before breakfast, twice. And every attic room in town was inspected, first of all, for the view.

On the porch, Aunt Polly kissed the top of two bright braids. "And what are you glad about today, my dear?" she asked, though she knew the answer. Pollyanna smiled up at her — the smile that had arrived with one small suitcase, years ago, and had never once left. "Everything," she said. "Just everything."
